clue.text: Set of posts in line dividing wetlands

indicators.note: something that divides an area sits inside it, splitting it in two

parts.note: a bog is a stretch of wet, spongy ground
L is the standard abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A row of fence posts runs in a line across a marsh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Posts' suggests wooden stakes, which suits the marsh picture, but here they are online entries, so the definition is a website of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A website made of a writer's dated online entries is called a blog; each entry is known as a post.

clue.text: Commanding Yorkshire's top region once

parts.note: to top something is to beat or best it
Yorkshire was historically divided into three administrative regions called Ridings
surface padding naming the county whose old divisions are meant

explanation.surface: Someone once held command over the highest part of Yorkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: The North, East and West Ridings of Yorkshire were the county's old divisions, abolished in 1974, hence 'once'.
explanation.definitionFit: To bestride something is to straddle and dominate it, so bestriding means towering over or controlling a situation.

clue.text: Old chap eating sprouts before Mass. He'll get complaints

indicators.note: what eats something takes it inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old
a chap is a man
buds are sprouts on a plant
M is the abbreviation for mass in physics

explanation.surface: An elderly man eats Brussels sprouts before church and is warned he will suffer the consequences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' just puts the sprouts ahead of the Mass inside the old chap. 'Complaints' plays on the windy effect of sprouts, but means formal grievances.
explanation.definitionFit: An ombudsman is an official appointed to investigate grievances that members of the public lodge against organisations.

clue.text: Rome's landfill, not filled evenly

indicators.note: in the Roman number system a letter stands for a value, so a letter is swapped for its number
'not' plus most of the word 'filled' tells us to take that stretch of letters away

parts.note: removing FIL from the middle leaves letters that read as 'L and L'
each L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A Roman rubbish tip has been only half filled.
explanation.walkthrough: Strip FIL from LANDFILL and the remainder reads as 'L and L'; Romans wrote fifty as L, so this gives fifty and fifty.
explanation.definitionFit: Split fifty-fifty means divided into two equal halves, which is sharing out evenly.

clue.text: Suffer endless public transport nightmare

indicators.note: without an end, a word loses its final letter

parts.note: to incur a loss is to suffer it
a bus is public transport

explanation.surface: A commuter endures an endless, nightmarish journey on public transport.
explanation.walkthrough: INCUR loses its last letter, then the bus follows.
explanation.definitionFit: An incubus is a demon thought to lie on sleepers, and by extension an oppressive nightmare or burden.

clue.text: In Wales a flower and in France a fabric

parts.note: the Taff is a river in Wales that flows through Cardiff; a 'flower' is something that flows
et is French for and
taken as written

explanation.surface: Wales is represented by a flower and France by a cloth, like national emblems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' reads as a bloom such as the daffodil, but in crosswords it is often a river, something that flows.
explanation.definitionFit: Taffeta is a crisp, lustrous woven cloth, usually silk, used for evening dresses.

clue.text: A tongue getting ready for something tasty

parts.note: French is a language, or tongue
dressing is putting clothes on to get ready

explanation.surface: A tongue is getting ready to taste something delicious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tongue' looks like the organ of taste, which fits the food picture, but it means a language.
explanation.definitionFit: This vinaigrette of oil and vinegar is poured over salads to add flavour, so it is a tasty extra.

clue.text: Strand story leads to Reichenbach eventually

parts.note: a fib is a story in the sense of a small lie

indicators.note: the leading letters are the ones at the very front of words

parts.note: the opening letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A Strand Magazine story leads to Sherlock Holmes's fall at the Reichenbach Falls.
explanation.walkthrough: The Holmes stories ran in The Strand Magazine, and Holmes apparently died at the Reichenbach Falls, so the surface is a nod to Conan Doyle.
explanation.definitionFit: A fibre is a single thread or filament, which is exactly what a strand is.

clue.text: A character from Ye Olden Days

indicators.note: a single character from a short word must be one of its letters, either the first or the last

parts.note: one possible character: the opening letter
since the character could be either letter, the choice itself is spelt out as the linking word between the alternatives
the other possible character: the closing letter

explanation.surface: Someone describes a figure from the quaint 'Ye Olden Days' of mock-medieval signs.
explanation.walkthrough: One character from YE is 'Y or E', and read straight through that is Y, OR, E.
explanation.definitionFit: Yore means time long past, as in the phrase 'days of yore', the same idea as old times.

clue.text: Maybe he makes firm declarations

parts.note: he is an example of a pronoun, hence 'maybe'
to cement something is to make it firm

explanation.surface: A man is perhaps the one making forceful official statements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He' looks like a person doing the declaring, but it is just a word, and an example of a part of speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Pronouncements are formal or authoritative statements, which is what declarations are.

clue.text: Serious Scots greeting one half-heartedly

indicators.note: doing something with only half a heart means losing half of the central part

parts.note: in Scots, to greet is to weep, so one who greets is a crier

explanation.surface: A Scotsman says hello to someone without much enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greeting' looks like saying hello, but in Scots it means crying. SOBBER has a double B at its heart; halve that and one B goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Sober can mean grave and solemn in manner, a synonym of serious.

clue.text: Anglican clutching iron rail in café

indicators.note: to clutch something is to hold it tightly, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: C of E, the Church of England, is the Anglican church
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
a rail is a bar

explanation.surface: A churchgoer grips an iron railing inside a café.
explanation.walkthrough: The iron goes right inside the church abbreviation, between its F and final E, before the rail is added.
explanation.definitionFit: A coffee bar is a small establishment serving coffee and snacks, which is another name for a café.

clue.text: Doctor without racket reportedly rents sports gear

indicators.note: 'without' in its old sense means outside, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: to doctor results is to rig them
a racket is a loud din

indicators.note: what is reported is heard rather than read, so we go by sound

parts.note: rents are tears or splits, which are breaches

explanation.surface: A quiet doctor rents out sporting equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' wants to mean lacking, but here it has its old sense of outside. 'Rents' looks like a verb about hiring; as a noun a rent is a tear.
explanation.definitionFit: Riding breeches are close-fitting trousers worn for horse riding, so they are clothing for an equestrian sport.

clue.text: Terms for the US border accepted by examiners

indicators.note: what is accepted is taken in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: examiners are testers
a rim is a border or edge

explanation.surface: Conditions for crossing the American frontier are agreed by inspectors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terms' and 'border' suggest a treaty at a frontier; in fact the terms are academic periods.
explanation.definitionFit: American schools and colleges often divide the year into three periods of study, each called a trimester.

clue.text: Killers perhaps, but not hard-nosed

parts.note: surface reading: murderers who are not hard-nosed, that is not tough or ruthless
setter's reading: lethal bullets whose noses are soft rather than hard, so they expand on impact

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard-nosed' wants to mean tough and unsentimental, which makes for gentle killers; read literally it is about the tip of a bullet.
explanation.definitionFit: Dumdum bullets are soft-nosed or hollow-pointed projectiles designed to expand on impact, causing deadly wounds.

clue.text: Examiner's car runs over detective

indicators.note: something placed over another covers it, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: an auto is a car
DI stands for Detective Inspector
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A driving examiner's car runs over a police detective.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs over' looks like a road accident; instead car and runs together go over, that is around, the detective.
explanation.definitionFit: An auditor officially examines accounts, so the word is a type of examiner.

clue.text: Offer to include upset batman down the order

indicators.note: to include something is to take it in, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: to tender is to offer
to ail someone is to trouble or upset them

explanation.surface: An offer is made to include a distressed batman in the lower part of a list.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batman' calls up the superhero or an officer's servant, but it means a batsman, a cricket batter. 'Upset' looks like an anagram signal, yet it simply means trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a tail-ender is one of the weaker batters placed last in the batting order.

clue.text: Caledonian ale's left brewing with high pH

indicators.note: brewing mixes and transforms ingredients, so the letters are reworked
something that has left has gone away, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, to be removed

explanation.surface: A Scottish beer has been left to brew and turned out alkaline.
explanation.walkthrough: Take ALE out of CALEDONIAN and rearrange the seven remaining letters. Caledonian is also a real Edinburgh brewery, which makes the surface plausible.
explanation.definitionFit: A substance with a high pH reading is alkaline, meaning it is not acidic.

clue.text: Did degrading act to get around test

indicators.note: to get around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: a deed is an act
the MOT is the annual roadworthiness test for vehicles in the UK

explanation.surface: Someone performed a humiliating act to get round an examination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Degrading' looks like describing the act as shameful; it is the definition, meaning lowering in rank.
explanation.definitionFit: To degrade someone in the old sense is to lower their rank, so having done that degrading is having demoted them.

clue.text: Coat worn by one in employment turning metal

indicators.note: turning round sends the letters back the other way
a garment worn by someone goes around them, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: a mac is a raincoat

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: employment of something is its use
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A worker turning metal on a lathe wears a protective coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning metal' suggests lathe work, but 'turning' reverses everything built before it. A mac, short for mackintosh, is a raincoat.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesium is a soft, highly reactive alkali metal, chemical element number 55.

clue.text: Trendy revolutionary dropped by friendly set

indicators.note: a revolution turns something right round, so the letters go backwards
what is dropped is let go, so those letters fall out

parts.note: something trendy is in
a congenial person is friendly

explanation.surface: A fashionable rebel is dropped by a sociable crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' sounds like a person but is the signal to turn the trendy word round. 'Set' looks like a group of people and is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To congeal is to thicken and become solid, as jelly or blood does when it sets.

clue.text: Statesmen impress with interim reshuffles

indicators.note: to reshuffle is to rearrange into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Political leaders win admirers with their temporary Cabinet reshuffles.
explanation.walkthrough: A Cabinet reshuffle is exactly what a prime minister does, so the anagram signal blends into the political picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Prime ministers are heads of government, which makes them leading political figures or statesmen.

clue.text: Uncompromising like Ireland's uprising

indicators.note: in a down answer, rising up means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: to dig something is slang for liking it
IR is the abbreviation for Ireland

explanation.surface: Someone is as unyielding as the Irish Easter Rising rebels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uprising' calls up the 1916 Easter Rising, but it is the signal to read upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone rigid in their views is inflexible and unwilling to bend, which is to be uncompromising.

clue.text: Screams of Hoxton's members of parliament

indicators.note: Hoxton is in London's East End, where a Cockney accent drops the opening H

parts.note: howls are loud screams

explanation.surface: An East London MP is screaming in the House of Commons.
explanation.walkthrough: A Cockney says 'owls' for HOWLS. 'Members of parliament' looks like politicians, but a parliament is the collective noun for owls.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of owls is called a parliament, so each bird is one of its members.

clue.text: Vehicle payment brings in zero after tax

indicators.note: to bring something in is to take it inside

parts.note: a wage is a payment for work
O looks like zero
nett, as in 'after tax', is pay with tax taken off

explanation.surface: A car allowance comes to nothing once tax is deducted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After tax' is one phrase for the take-home amount, not an order instruction. Nett is the British spelling of net.
explanation.definitionFit: A wagonette is a four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage with facing side seats, so it is a kind of vehicle.

clue.text: Central digit poking bare elbow

indicators.note: something poking into another goes inside it

parts.note: bare means nude

indicators.note: the central part of a word is its middle letter

parts.note: the middle of the five letters

explanation.surface: A middle finger jabs into an uncovered elbow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elbow' looks like the body part being poked, which suits the digit; it is a verb, meaning to jostle.
explanation.definitionFit: To elbow someone is to push them with the elbow, and a nudge is a gentle push of exactly that kind.

clue.text: A way to ride in teams to confuse

parts.note: teams in a match are sides
to addle is to muddle or confuse

explanation.surface: Riding in teams is a way to cause confusion.
explanation.walkthrough: SIDES and ADDLE simply join; 'to' just leads into the second piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Riding sidesaddle means sitting with both legs on one side of the horse, a traditional style for women riders.

clue.text: Resentful about God

indicators.note: to turn about is to face the other way

parts.note: feeling sore about something is feeling resentful

explanation.surface: Someone feels bitter about God.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as 'concerning', but it means turn round.
explanation.definitionFit: Eros is the Greek god of love, counterpart of the Roman Cupid.
